item.text:
“I’ll see you tomorrow,” you tell Owen.

“Maybe in the afternoon. Depends on the trains.”

His timer sounds again. He drains his tea, takes the toolbox and returns to the counter fittings without trying to prolong the break.

You go out through the side door alone and follow the lane down towards the harbour. The cinema stands only one road back from the water; within a minute, the smell of plaster and cardboard gives way to salt, diesel and wet rope.

The tide sits halfway down the harbour wall. Fishing boats are tied two deep along the inner quay, their hulls lifting against black rubber fenders. One crewman hoses silver scales from a row of plastic boxes while gulls patrol the roof of the packing depot. Across the water, a travel lift holds a blue boat above the boatyard concrete, its propeller dripping steadily.

You follow the quay past stacked lobster pots and a bench facing the harbour mouth. The restored Picture House sign is visible above the roofs behind you, its cream lettering unlit in the daylight.

At the harbour office, a chalkboard lists the week’s high tides. Beyond it, the outer breakwater reaches into rougher water, but your short route turns along the inner basin instead. Wind presses at your carefully mended coat and rattles halyards against aluminium masts.

No one joins you or calls you into conversation. You complete the harbour circuit at your own pace, then climb Harbour Street back towards the cinema. The walk takes the remainder of your break, and you return to the side entrance before your catalogue work resumes.
